newsitem.title: LEBANON: Union leader's arrest raises protests in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Union leader's arrest raises protests in Lebanon.

text.p: The Lebanese government faced a storm of protest on Monday over the weekend arrest of a fiery labour leader who has been a thorn in the side of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri for several years.
A senior church leader said the arrest of leftist Elias Abou Rizk on Friday was a matter of personal revenge.
A former prime minister said it was politically motivated and a step on the road to dictatorship in Lebanon.

Abou Rizk, 54, was charged with impersonating the head of the General Labour Confederation (CGTL) and forcibly usurping office after disputed elections in April which split the labour movement and produced two rival CGTL leaderships.

The charges against Abou Rizk, who led a campaign of anti-government strikes and protests as CGTL leader from 1993-1997, were brought by his rival Ghneim al-Zoghbi whom the government recognised in April as the new head of the CGTL.
The charges carry jail terms of at least seven years.

Abou Rizk, who accused Hariri of ignoring social issues in his multi-billion dollars drive to rebuild Lebanon after the 1975-90 civil war, spent the weekend under detention in hospital suffering from high blood pressure after a magistrate ordered his arrest for pre-trial interrogation.
Church leaders, newspapers, opposition politicians and intellectuals denounced his arrest as a violation of union freedoms and political rights.
"Abou Rizk's arrest has snowballed into an explosive political issue at home and a case of freedoms and human rights for the rest of the world," the conservative daily an-Nahar said.

Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, the Maronite patriarch and Lebanon's most outspoken figure on democracy and human rights, said in a Sunday sermon the issue was besmirching the civilised image that Pope John Paul's visit gave Lebanon last month.
Archbishop Elias Audi of the Greek Orthodox church, of which Abou Rizk is a member, said people in Lebanon were now fearful for their freedoms.
"They are shutting peoples' mouths on the basis of personal revenge, not on the basis of national good," Audi said in a comment on Abouu Rizk's arrest.
"We hope no one will say to us they have eyes but they do not see and ears but they do not hear," Audi said.

A group of 50 intellectuals including university professors, media personalities and lawyers said in a protest the arrest was "part of a campaign by the government against the General Labour Confederation, labour freedoms and political freedoms".
Former prime minister Omar Karami was quoted by an-Nahar as saying it was politically motivated and likely to rebound by making Abou Rizk a major political leader in the country.
Asked if the arrest signalled a move towards dictatorship in Lebanon, Karami said: "Sure, this is just the beginning".
